short_summary: This comprehensive article explores the molecular mechanisms, advanced analytical techniques, and clinical applications of food sensory perception. It begins by detailing the biological pathways of taste, smell, and chemesthesis, highlighting the roles of G protein-coupled receptors, ion channels, and Transient Receptor Potential channels. The review then transitions to flavoromics, examining how advanced instrumental methods like gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS), and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy decode complex flavor profiles. Furthermore, it compares traditional human sensory evaluation panels with innovative electronic sensors, such as electronic noses and tongues, and biometric measurements. The article emphasizes the integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and multi-omics data to predict sensory attributes from chemical structures. Ultimately, these insights bridge fundamental discovery with translational applications, enabling advancements in personalized nutrition, food quality control, and pharmaceutical taste masking.
long_summary: This extensive review provides a deep dive into the molecular basis of flavor perception, integrating biological mechanisms with state-of-the-art analytical chemistry and data science. Flavor is a multisensory experience combining gustation, olfaction, and somatosensation. The article meticulously details the receptor-level interactions responsible for the five basic tastes, sweet, umami, and bitter via G protein-coupled receptors (T1R and T2R families), and salty and sour via specific ion channels. It also explores the olfactory system's odorant receptors and the trigeminal nerve pathways mediating chemesthesis through Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels. Genetic variations in these receptors are discussed, explaining individual differences in taste sensitivity and their implications for personalized nutrition and pharmaceutical compliance. Transitioning from biology to analytical chemistry, the text highlights the emerging field of flavoromics. It evaluates high-throughput instrumental techniques, particularly gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for volatile aroma profiling, liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) for non-volatile tastants, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy for structural elucidation. To correlate these chemical profiles with human perception, the article contrasts traditional sensory evaluation methods, such as Quantitative Descriptive Analysis (QDA) and difference testing, with innovative technologies. Electronic noses, electronic tongues, and biometric sensors offer rapid, objective alternatives to human panels, minimizing subjective biases. Furthermore, the review addresses the computational challenges of integrating multi-omics data. It showcases how artificial intelligence and machine learning, including graph neural networks and diffusion models, are revolutionizing flavor prediction by decoding complex structure-odor relationships. Standardized methodologies from ISO and ASTM are emphasized to ensure reproducibility across studies. Ultimately, this comprehensive synthesis of molecular biology, advanced analytics, and AI-driven modeling offers critical insights for researchers and industry professionals, driving innovations in food science, quality authentication, and the development of palatable therapeutic agents.
